Why Not a Bare Timer?

The SLA monitor from CLAUDE.md's domain events — and why setInterval isn't good enough to build it on.

CLAUDE.md's domain events end with one that's different from the other four: "a BullMQ-scheduled SLA-breach scan." ticket.created, ticket.assigned, ticket.commented, and ticket.status_changed (Week 5) all fire because a request came in and a service handled it. The SLA monitor has no request to react to — it has to notice, on its own, that a ticket has sat open too long, which means something has to keep checking on a schedule.

The obvious first idea is a plain setInterval, running right inside the API process:

// Not real code — the shape this would take with no queue at all.
setInterval(async () => {
  // ...find overdue tickets, escalate them...
}, 60 * 60 * 1000);

This looks simple, but everything about it is fragile in a way that matters more here than it might elsewhere:

  • It dies with the process. Restart the API (a deploy, a crash, npm run dev's own --watch reload) and the timer is gone until the process comes back up — there's no record anywhere that a scan was even supposed to have happened while it was down.
  • A thrown error inside it is silent. An uncaught rejection in the callback doesn't retry, doesn't get logged anywhere obvious, and doesn't stop the next tick from running — it just quietly skipped one scan.
  • It runs inside the same process serving HTTP traffic. A slow scan (many tickets, a slow query) competes with the API for the same event loop.

A real job queue — BullMQ, backed by Redis — solves all three by moving "a scan needs to happen" out of process memory and into Redis instead: a scheduled job is a row of state something else can see, retry, and hand to a different process to actually run. That last part is the one this lesson leans on hardest — see "Queues and Workers" next.
